stories.title: Minister rules out extension to developer levy waiver
stories.summary: The Minister for Housing has put pressure on developers to finish new homes by the end of this year by insisting an existing waiver on water connections and developer levies will not be extended past December. James Browne said while the existing waiver, which was introduced two years ago, has helped to speed up developments, there is no possibility it will be extended into 2027. It is a reiteration of previous Department of Housing statements, but is believed to be an attempt to force developers to speed up construction in the final two months of this year - a move that will in turn increase the official and highly politicised annual housing and apartment construction rate. The waiver was first introduced in 2024 and means developers do not have to pay for water connections or a levy on newly constructed developments if they are finished by the end of 2026 with the State instead paying these costs. It was intended to encourage developers to speed up the construction of new houses and apartments in order to avail of the financial support. After the Central Statistics Office reported the construction of new homes has increased this year - with 26,833 homes built between January and September compared with 24,256 homes in the same period last year - Mr Browne said the increase is the highest since the CSO began to count these figures and is a sign that policies like the levy waiver are working.

stories.title: PTSB reports 7% rise in total operating income for Q3
stories.summary: PTSB has reported higher income for the third quarter of this year and said it remains confident about its prospects for the rest of the year. In a trading update for the three months to the end of September, PTSB said it continued to see strong momentum with total operating income up 7%. The bank, which agreed earlier this year to be bought by Austrian bank BAWAG, said that total gross customer loans rose to €23.4 billion, up €0.8 billion year to date and over 4% on an annual basis. The lender said the increase was driven by its core mortgage book which gained momentum as the year has progressed. New mortgage lending rose by 10% and PTSB said its share of new mortgage business was about 20% for the first nine months of 2026. It added that it has a strong pipeline heading into the fourth quarter. Meanwhile, new Business Banking Lending (SME and Asset Finance) rose up 16% in the three month period.

stories.title: LOI preview: Last orders before final whistle of season
stories.summary: After 267 days, another SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division season is coming to an end tonight. When the campaign kicked off in earnest on 6 February, some of the main questions included whether Shamrock Rovers could retain the crown they had regained in 2025; could Derry City push forward with hometown hero James McClean in tow; were Dundalk ready for a return to the top flight; and who would be involved in the battle to avoid the drop? As 7.45pm approaches tonight, almost all of the matters of importance have been resolved with a week to spare. Shamrock Rovers will lift the title they secured this day last week, while their closest pursuers Bohemians and St Patrick's Athletic booked their spots in Europe a long time ago which will be some consolation - particularly financially - after falling short in the latter part of the run-in. Sligo Rovers have long known that they will be playing First Division football in 2027, and only a huge swing in goal difference will save Drogheda United from the relegation play-off spot if they can pick up three points and Waterford lose elsewhere. For Stephen Bradley and Shamrock Rovers, they fully intend to put a final layer of icing on the cake when they face Dundalk at Oriel Park tonight before they get their hands on the league trophy.

stories.title: What makes a great horror movie so scary?
stories.summary: Analysis: Halloween is a great time watch a scary movie, but what's the science behind why we keep watching even when it scares us? This article is now available as a Brainstorm podcast and can be heard above. You can also subscribe to the Brainstorm podcast through Apple Podcasts, Stitcher, Spotify or wherever you get your podcasts. We are essentially seeking cheap thrills when we watch horror movies. Like riding roller-coasters, scary films allow us to experience heightened sensations, but in relative safety. Brain-mapping experiments have helped reveal that neural networks controlling fear and anxiety are activated in subjects watching horror films. The subsequent release of stress hormones like dopamine, adrenaline and cortisol in our bodies is an experience many of us evidently enjoy. Clearly, horror movies aim to stimulate this fight-or-flight biological reaction to perceived danger, but how do they achieve this? It is no surprise that the horror genre is filled with creatures hell-bent on devouring people. Humans may be the predominant species on the planet, but it is not that long in evolutionary terms since we lived in much greater danger of predation from larger, fiercer creatures. A fear of being eaten, or bitten, by animals is effectively hard-wired into our psyche. Eye-tracking studies have shown that even children are quicker to spot pictures of threatening animals, compared to harmless objects, demonstrating humans have an in-built awareness of danger in nature. Documentary On One Hallowe'en special with extracts and short docs from the archive to mark the spookiest night of the year. Thus, monster movies effectively trigger those survival instincts which we have developed as a species. That involuntary yelp we emit during scary moments is basically a warning signal to others about nearby danger. Likewise, fear of infection, followed by sickness or death, is another deep-rooted human dread which we have inherited from our ancestors who didn’t have medicine to save them. Notably, all of our favourite movie monsters, like werewolves, vampires and zombies bite their victims. Our collective human experience through history means we are instinctively repulsed by such actions onscreen.

stories.title: US DJ Marc Kinchen on why he turned down Taylor Swift
stories.summary: He's worked with everyone from Beyoncé to Elton John and from Rihanna to Celine Dion but US DJ Marc Kinchen says he turned down a chance to do a remix for Taylor Swift. The 54-year-old Detroit native, who is better known as MK, has been putting his own spin on major acts, dance-adjacent or not, since the early nineties - an era when a bonus track dance remix from a name DJ was a must, back when the humble CD single ruled the charts. However, radical changes in how people listen to music and how music is actually produced mean MK no longer sees the allure of big bucks offers to work with big name rock and pop stars. "I said no to a Taylor Swift remix. Hahaha," he laughs. "When you're doing dance remixes, you don’t want to make the wrong turn and have some diehards who are into the underground dance music scene, stuff that is so anti-pop music, moan about it. "In my younger days I would have jumped at doing a remix for Taylor Swift but I just thought it wasn’t the right career move to take Taylor Swift, the ultimate pop artist, and try to make a cool dance record with one of her songs. It just didn’t feel right, it just didn’t feel right. That stuff definitely worked in the nineties." Of course, it was a different world back then and MK has seen styles and trends come and go.

stories.title: Trump scraps last two election rallies ahead of midterms
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is scrapping two of his last midterm election rallies, his Republican Party has said, as the 80-year-old leader lashed out at a reporter who asked if he was tired of travelling. Instead of the events in Kansas and Iowa, Mr Trump will hold a "large number" of virtual "telerallies" in a series of states, the Republican National Committee (RNC) said. Republicans are fighting to keep control of Congress in the 3 November midterms. Mr Trump has urged the party to "pretend I'm on the ballot" to maximise turnout despite his poor approval ratings. "With Republicans in a strong position in Kansas and Iowa, previously planned in-person rallies in those states will no longer take place as scheduled," the RNC statement said. Mr Trump's final election rally is now set to be in Florida today.

stories.title: Intel shares tumble after hours, hit by chip supply woes
stories.summary: Intel shares plunged 23% in after hours trading on Wall Street last night after the chip maker warned it would burn cash this year due to the faltering PC market, bottlenecks in manufacturing and heavy spending on expanding production. Like many other major tech companies, Intel has been pouring money into manufacturing, but has run into supply disruptions that have capped its ability to capitalise on growing demand for data-centre chips. Compounding that pressure, PC costs are on the rise due to the surge in memory prices, which has weighed on demand. That weak demand could persist through the first half of 2027, Intel warned, as it also forecast December-quarter revenue below market expectations. Intel expects the deadly October explosion at its Israel plant to erase roughly $600m in revenue over two quarters and reduce supplies of AI server chips to cloud customers, Intel told Reuters in an interview. "I'm disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter," Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on a conference call with analysts.

stories.title: AFCON to be held every two years after CAF U-turn
stories.summary: The Africa Cup of Nations will be held every two years, not four as was planned, governing body the Confederation ⁠of African Football (CAF) announced after reversing an earlier decision. AFCON has traditionally been staged every two years, but CAF's surprise decision last December to move to a four-year cycle was not widely welcomed. "The Confederation of African Football (CAF) Executive Committee today unanimously decided that the CAF Africa Cup of Nations will return to taking place every two years," ‌CAF said in ⁠a statement. Under the previous plan, AFCON would have moved to a four-year cycle, with the proposed CAF Nations League becoming the continent's biennial competition. stories.title: Are these the 5 most terrifying songs ever recorded?
stories.summary: Analysis: Forget Thriller and the Monster Mash, here are 5 tunes which are truly unsettling, disturbing and haunting As plastic skeletons enter the shops, pumpkin spice flavourings spread through coffee houses like Japanese knot-weed and jumpers are dug out of drawers, music fans' playlists also begin to shift, with "spooky sounds" replacing "sunshine mixes". Just as Christmas means endless repeats of Mistletoe & Wine and Fairytale of New York, the arrival of autumn means Thriller and the Monster Mash. But while such songs might be described as "spoopy" (internet slang describing cute, comical, or silly versions of typically spooky subject matter), they're not exactly unsettling. This Halloween, if you want to put the "k" back in "spooky", these are the tracks for you. Listen if you dare ... The majority of Rubber Ring isn't in the least bit spooky. But towards the outro, a female voice appears under Morrissey's vocal, repeating the line: "You are sleeping, you do not want to believe." The sample was taken from the flexi-disc accompaniment to the book Breakthrough: An Amazing Experiment in Electronic Communication with the Dead (1971) by Latvian psychologist Konstantin Raudive. The book put forward a theory that deceased communicators appear to send messages and images via computers, radios, televisions and other electronic devices. The voice we hear is a real-time English translation of the alleged ghost voice of Raudive's mentor Gephardt Frye, speaking in Swedish and German. And it makes me shiver every time I hear it.

stories.title: Michael Douglas opens up about relationship with Kirk
stories.summary: Two-time Academy Award winning actor Michael Douglas has opened up about his fraught relationship with his screen legend father Kirk. Wall Street and Fatal Attraction star Michael (82) recently published his new book One Helluva Ride in which he reflects on his 60-year film career and reveals much about his private life including how his father, who died aged 103 in 2020, once told him he was a "terrible actor". "In the third act of his life, when he had a helicopter crash and was recovering, he became more religious and turned to the Old Testament and studied that. "He became more spiritual and kind and as happens to a lot of people as their career dwindles, you get more time to focus on your family and we were very close. "I admired him. Most people haven't had a father like Spartacus, larger than life. You just question whether you can ever be the man that he is." In One Helluva Ride, Douglas says his father was less than complimentary about his son’s acting skills at the start of his career.

stories.title: Mary O'Sullivan on celebrating Limerick through her designs
stories.summary: Charlotte Ryan speaks to Limerick designer Mary O'Sullivan about immortalising Irish locations through heritage techniques, and how her daughter became her 'why'. You may have already seen O'Sullivan's regal designs, from the breathtaking green column dress worn by Limerick Rose for 2025 Leah McMahon, to Roz Purcell, who strode down the runway at the Ireland Fashion Week 'Irish Roots' show this year in a corseted mini dress emblazoned with sights from across Ireland. What unites these designs is O'Sullivan's reimagining of a classic textile design: toile de jouy, an 18th-century technique featuring bucolic scenes printed on linen or cotton in shades of blue or deep red. A highly fashionable choice for aristocratic interiors, as historian Laura Fitzachary writes, it was championed by Marie Antoinette and Empress Josephine. But O'Sullivan's version is decidedly for a different kind of fashion lover: the kind that sees romance in a perfect pint, who loves a visit to Costello's pub in Limerick City, who might wear a silk scarf with their trackies, and who deeply values the work of homegrown creators. She is one of a number of Irish designers making waves in the fashion industry, both at home and abroad, signalling a future of innovation and a unique visual language that draws from our history.

stories.title: Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved' Patrick Stewart
stories.summary: Ian McKellen has led tributes to Patrick Stewart following his death from Alzheimer's disease, calling him "the most respected and beloved actor of his generation". Stewart - famed for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in later versions of Star Trek - died at his home in Los Angeles, it was announced on social media yesterday. McKellen, who held a long friendship with Stewart, said the actor "was defined by being born and bred in Yorkshire". In a statement posted to social media, McKellen said: "You could hear it in his accented voice and in the stern honesty with which he told you what he thought and felt. "Yorkshiremen have no truck with half-truths or avoidance of big issues. He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love." McKellen said one of his strongest memories of the actor was cautioning him against starring in science-fiction.

stories.title: Bank of Japan says inflation hit 2% target after 13 years
stories.summary: The Bank of Japan said today that inflation had hit its 2% target, more than 13 years after it adopted the goal in a bid to pull the economy out of deflation, but held off hiking interest rates for now. Successive governments struggled for decades to pull the country out of a spiral of deflation - sustained falls in prices that are harmful for economic growth - and the 2% goal was set in 2013 as the Bank of Japan launched massive monetary easing measures. While core consumer inflation intermittently topped the level in the early 2020s, today marked the first time that the central bank confirmed the long-term price trend had been achieved. "Underlying CPI (consumer price index) inflation is at a level that is generally consistent with the price stability target of two percent, and is expected to remain at around that level," the central bank said on its website. Despite the central bank's view of sustainable inflation, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government has been more cautious about officially declaring victory over deflation. "We're not there," Economy Minister Minoru Kiuchi said last week.

stories.title: 3,300 in Kerry town without safe drinking water for weeks
stories.summary: Over 3,300 people in Ballyheigue in Co Kerry have been without safe drinking water for over three weeks - following a 'do not consume' notice issued by Uisce Éireann on 7 October. The notice was issued after saltwater was detected in the raw water source supplying Ballyheigue’s water treatment plant. It is believed to be the first major incident of saltwater intrusion into a deep underground aquifer in Ireland. Under the notice, affected residents have been advised not to use their water for drinking, food preparation, or brushing teeth, with a particular warning to children under 12 months. Neither domestic water filters or boiling the water will make it safe to drink, while it can still be used for personal hygiene, bathing, flushing toilets, laundry and washing of utensils. Yesterday, dozens of Ballyheigue residents picked up alternative water supplies in the form of bottles and a tanker, provided by Uisce Éireann.

stories.title: Maguire and Walsh struggle at the Maybank Championship
stories.summary: Irish duo Leona Maguire and Lauren Walsh both struggled to make an impact during the second round of the Maybank Championship on Friday. Japan's Miyu Yamashita took sole lead of the tournament in Malaysia as her round of 66 saw her finish the day on 13 under par to leapfrog first-round leader Pauline Roussin-Bouchard. Roussin-Bouchard wasn't able to match her blistering opening-round form and signed for a 69 which leaves her on 11 under alongside Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez. At the other end of the leaderboard, Maguire and Walsh will be grateful that there's no midway cut at this tournament. Maguire, starting on the 10th hole, was up against it from the very beginning as she hit a double bogey at her first hole. Her form was up and down after that as four birdies were cancelled out by three bogeys and she eventually signed for a round of 73 that leaves her on one over.

stories.title: Call for supports as number of Irish growers plummets
stories.summary: The country's fruit and vegetable producers are calling for more support from retailers and the Government to address an alarming decline in the number of commercial growers in recent decades. Since the 1990s, it is estimated that the number of commercial growers here has plunged from over 600 to around 70. "We're down to five tomato growers, large-scale tomato growers in Ireland," said Martin Flynn, whose family has been growing tomatoes near Swords in north Co Dublin since the 1960s. The third-generation grower said "that's predominantly due to the cost of getting into the sector and the level of investment needed to build modern glasshouses… a hectare of glass costs €2.5m to build. "You need long-term contracts, long-term commitment from retailers and also you need to be supported at Government level in terms of the massive problems we're seeing with energy prices." Mr Flynn said the profit margins "are so tight you need to keep reinvesting".

stories.title: Mushroom killer loses appeal, given harsher sentence
stories.summary: Australian mushroom killer Erin Patterson has failed to overturn a slew of convictions, and a judge instead imposed a heavier prison sentence for three "cold and calculated" poisoning murders. Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering her husband's parents and aunt in 2023, deliberately lacing their beef Wellington lunch with lethal death cap mushrooms. The strange nature of what had been dubbed the "mushroom murders" fuelled intense global interest, with Patterson's 11-week trial drawing more publicity than almost any other Australian case in recent memory. Patterson maintained her triple murder convictions were a "miscarriage of justice", urging the Court of Appeal in Victoria state to either set her free or have the case heard again. But the court not only threw out her bid to have the convictions quashed, it found her "carefully planned and deliberate" killings deserved an even harsher sentence. "This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated," judge Stephen McLeish said as he dismissed Patterson's appeal.

stories.title: NFL: Love conquers all for the Green Bay Packers
stories.summary: Jordan Love passed for three touchdowns and the Green Bay Packers turned back a fourth-quarter rally for a 27-19 victory over the Carolina Panthers. Carolina, who trailed 27-10 in the third quarter, rallied within 27-19 with 5:37 remaining in the game when Bryce Young hit Jalen Coker with a 26-yard touchdown pass on fourth-and-3. The two-point conversion pass was incomplete. The Panthers (3-4) got the ball back at their own 45 after a punt with 4:35 left, but Young's fourth-down pass was incomplete. Carolina got a final possession starting at its own 20 with 22 seconds left, but Young was sacked once and Green Bay picked off a lateral on the final play. Love completed 30 of 41 passes for 288 yards with one interception in addition to his three touchdowns. Packers receiver Christian Watson, who left the stadium in an ambulance for testing after sustaining a first-half chest injury, returned to action in the third quarter and finished with eight catches for 113 yards. Green Bay (5-3), which entered last in the NFL in rushing at 59.9 yards per game, managed just 66 yards on the ground. Josh Jacobs, in his second game since coming off the commissioner exempt list following an offseason incident, had 39 yards on 21 attempts (1.9 yards per carry). The Packers are the first team in NFL history with a a winning record through eight games while having less than 500 rushing yards on the season.

stories.summary: Iowa is at the heart of the American agricultural industry, but the Trump administration has opened up fresh challenges for farmers. "It's really high stress," said Matt Russell, Executive Director of the Iowa Farmers Union, which represents around 1,000 members. Tariffs and the war in Iran have created trade uncertainty and pushed up costs ahead of next week's midterm elections. "All that disruption has been incredibly difficult for farming families," said Mr Russell. "So, in Iowa, we're corn, soybeans, beef ... On top of that, you have fertiliser, you have chemicals, you have diesel fuel. "All of those inputs have really ratcheted up, and then interest rates are also a big part of this."

stories.title: Dobey wins in Den Bosch as O'Connor makes semi-final run
stories.summary: Ireland's Willie O'Connor made an impressive run to the semi-finals at Players Championship 32 but it was England's Chris Dobey who went all the way to victory in Den Bosch, Netherlands on Thursday. Dobey beat Tommy Morris 8-4 to wrap up his third ranking title of the season. Matches between Tom Sykes and Cor Dekker, Bradley Brooks and Adam Gawlas, and Wesley Plaisier and Damon Heta all produced nine-dart finishes in Den Bosch. Dobey averaged 103.15 across his seven matches, registering the three highest averages of the afternoon on his way to the win. Meanwhile, Limerick native O'Connor posted 100-plus averages to first beat Martin Schindler 6-4 and then Niels Zonneveld 6-5 in the last-16. His quarter-final victory over Karel Sedlacek by the same score also saw him convert an excellent 148 finish.

stories.title: Netanyahu bloc ahead in vote, but well short of majority
stories.summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp has finished ahead of the opposition but remained well short of a majority, final results from Israel's general election showed, setting the stage for tough coalition talks or potentially another vote. Mr Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with his Likud party remaining the largest faction with 27 seats. The opposition bloc, led by centrist Gadi Eisenkot, secured 48 seats. The results from the Central Elections Committee also cemented the emergence as potential kingmakers of the Arab party groupings Ra'am and the Joint List, with the two winning a combined 19 seats. stories.title: Manosphere must be treated as public health risk - report
stories.summary: The so-called manosphere should be addressed as a public health problem with harms caused online tackled in a similar way to the tobacco industry, academics have argued. The authors of a new report defined the manosphere as "a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation". They argued the movement - which centres around a so-called crisis of masculinity and a shared conviction that feminism has systematically disadvantaged men - has contributed to many health harms. These include violence against women and girls, and mental health issues, as well as "delegitimising" the idea of boys and men seeking help. Outrage and grievance are "good for business" in this online environment, the authors said, with boys and young men especially having their insecurities cultivated in the manosphere and subsequently monetised. Their report, published in medical journal The Lancet, said: "Similar to the tobacco and ultra processed food industries, content creators and hosting platforms deploy strategies that individualise responsibility.

stories.title: Furlong cleared of foul play by disciplinary committee
stories.summary: Leinster's Tadhg Furlong has been cleared of any foul play following an incident with Munster's Gavin Coombes during their United Rugby Championship match last Saturday. Coombes alleged during the game that his testicles had been grabbed and despite match referee Andrew Brace asking the TMO Colin Stanley to review the incident at the time, neither could find evidence of the incident. However, the incident was included in the referee's report and subsequently reviewed by the citing commissioner Peter Ferguson. Furlong appeared in front of an independent disciplinary committee - comprising of Simon Thomas (Wales), Attie Heyns (South Africa) and Pamela Woodman (Scotland) that "unanimously concluded that the citing complaint against the Player should be dismissed, on the basis that he did not commit an act of foul play contrary to Law 9.27." Despite the dismissal of the complaint, the disciplinary committee concluded that Coombes had given "an honest account of his recollection of events surrounding the incident." Furlong will available for selections for Ireland's Nations Championship campaign next month where Andy Farrell’s men will take on Argentina, Fiji, South Africa and one other team on Saturday, 28 November.

stories.title: S Korea to prosecute students cheating with smart glasses
stories.summary: South Korea will file criminal complaints against students caught cheating on a national university entrance exam with smart glasses and toughen penalties for their use, a government official has said. Sales of smart glasses - which allow the wearer to shoot photos and videos, and interact with an AI assistant among other abilities - are growing worldwide. But so is a backlash around the gadgets, including concerns over people being filmed without consent and their use by exam cheats. South Korea's notoriously gruelling college entry exam, known as the "Suneung", is essential for admission to top universities and widely regarded as a gateway to economic security and even a good marriage. "The ministry will seek criminal charges against students caught cheating with smart glasses" in the future, Lee Joon-hyuk, an education ministry official, told AFP. Under authorities' plans, students caught cheating with smart glasses will not be able to retake their exams for three years, an extension from the current penalty of one year.

A second planned strike was suspended to allow for talks, however industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule is continuing across the public sector. Yesterday, Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris said he was hopeful the talks would conclude in the coming days and that there would be an agreement. "That's really what everybody is working to try and achieve."

stories.title: Gallagher and Reilly come in as Ireland make two changes
stories.summary: Niamh Gallagher and Aoibheann Reilly have both been handed starts for Ireland's final WXV Global Series game of the season. The pair are the only changes made by head coach Scott Bemand for Saturday's rematch with South Africa in Cape Town. Gallagher comes in at full-back with Reilly starting at scrum-half, as Stacey Flood and Emily Lane swap to the bench after last week's 40-27 win. Sophie Barrett comes into the matchday 23 also, in place of Ulster teammate Sadhbh McGrath. It's an unchanged pack for Ireland, with Linda Djougang and Eilís Cahill packing down either side of hooker Neve Jones, with Dorothy Wall and Jane Clohessy in the second row. Erin King captains the side once again at openside flanker, with Fiona Tuite-O'Sullivan on the blindside, and Brittany Hogan packing down at number 8. Reilly comes in at scrum-half for her 24th cap, while Dannah O'Brien starts for the 21st Test in a row at out-half.
